1: A wealthy man returned to find his great mansion in flames, and his children inside, absorbed in their games. He cried out: Run, children, the house is burning! But they did not hear him, so absorbed were they in play. Then the father called: Children, come quickly! I have toys — ox-carts, goat-carts, deer-carts — all waiting outside! And at the word 'carts' they ran out, and were saved.

The Buddha said to Shariputra: Even as that elder, using the play of carts, saved his children from the burning house, so the Tathagata, knowing the world is a burning house, uses every skilful means to draw beings out of it. The teachings are many, but the goal is one: the vehicle of the Buddha, in which all beings arrive at the same awakening.

Know this, O Shariputra: the Enlightened One teaches the dharma to beings by means of parables, and by every form of skilful action. The word of the Buddha is never false; and the day shall come when every one of these beings shall attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
2: A son left his father and wandered for fifty years in poverty. At last, worn and ragged, he came to the city where his father had grown rich — and did not know him. The father knew his son at once, and sent servants who seized him; the son fainted with terror, thinking he was to be punished. So the father released him, and for years employed him secretly at humble work, until the son could bear kindness, and at the end was told the truth: You are my son, and all I have is yours.
[Lotus Sutra, ch. 4 — The treasure in the robe]

Like a friend who, parting from a poor man, sews a jewel into the hem of his garment without his knowing — and the poor man wanders, begging, the jewel always with him — so beings carry the treasure of awakening in the robe of their own nature, and do not know it.
[Lotus Sutra, ch. 5 — The rain on all plants]

The cloud rains on every plant alike — on the great trees and the small herbs, on the roots of the sweetest flowers and the roots of the bitterest weeds. The rain is one; the growth is each according to its nature. So is the teaching of the Buddha: one rain of the dharma, and every being grows in its own season.
3: [Lotus Sutra, ch. 12 — The daughter of the dragon king]

Then the daughter of the dragon king, eight years old, wise beyond her years, came before the Buddha and offered him a jewel worth a whole world. Before the jewel reached his hand, she said: See, I have turned into a Buddha — my awakening is not slower than yours. And she taught: In my person there is no barrier; I can attain Buddhahood — so why should you say a woman's body is an obstacle?

A physician went abroad and his children, left alone, took poison in their father's absence. He returned and cried out in grief, and mixed for them a medicine of rare virtue. Some took it and were healed; the rest, in their delirium, refused. So the father announced that he was dying, and left a message — and at the news, the remaining children came to their senses, took the medicine, and lived. The Buddha said: So do I teach as one who seems to pass away, that beings may treasure the teaching while it remains.
[Lotus Sutra, ch. 25 — The one who hears the cries]

If beings who are drowning call on the name of the one who hears the cries of the world, the wind and the waves shall be stilled. If they fall into a pit of fire, the fire shall become a pool. For he who made the vow to hear every cry does not arrive late; the gate of his compassion is open on every side.
